clue.text: See 2 if confused about final two parts of clues

indicators.note: something confused is jumbled out of order, so the letters of the referenced entry get mixed up
the closing pair of letters of the following word are all that is kept

blocks.note: the answer to 2 down, the baseball team
the last two letters of the word clues

explanation.surface: A cross-reference telling a puzzled solver where to look for help with how clues end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See 2' reads like an ordinary pointer to another clue, but See is the definition and 2 stands for that entry's answer, mixed up along with the ending of clues.
explanation.definitionFit: To witness something is to observe it happening, a synonym for the verb see.

clue.text: Sexist metaphor: he wants "a pert bombshell"

indicators.note: a bombshell blows things apart, so the letters it hits land in a new order

explanation.surface: A chauvinist's figure of speech about a man's desire for a saucy, glamorous woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Bombshell looks like the glamorous woman of the quote, but it is the signal to rearrange the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying someone wears the pants means they are in charge, a phrase that assumes control is properly a man's.

clue.text: Ties at first, then victories for baseball team

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word it follows

explanation.surface: A sports-page summary of a team's record: some drawn games early on, then a run of wins.
explanation.walkthrough: The Minnesota Twins are a Major League Baseball team.
explanation.definitionFit: The Twins are a Major League club based in Minneapolis, an example of a baseball team.

clue.text: Erudite fellow getting up to embrace actress Blanchett

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means the word is read from bottom to top
to embrace is to hold something inside one's arms, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: a dude is a fellow, a guy

explanation.surface: A learned man, rising in the world, gets to put his arms round a film star.
explanation.walkthrough: DUDE turned upwards becomes EDUD, which then has CATE put inside it after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An erudite person is well read and learned, which is what educated means.

clue.text: Sage's torn panties

indicators.note: torn fabric is ripped apart, so the letters are pulled into a new order

explanation.surface: A wise man's underwear has been ripped, or the herb sage's frilly lingerie has.
explanation.walkthrough: Sage looks like a noun, a wise man or the herb, but it is the adjective meaning wise; the 's is just 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapient is a literary adjective for wise, the same sense as sage used as an adjective.

clue.text: Filthy locale outside university, very loud and poorly ventilated

indicators.note: one thing being outside another means it wraps around it

blocks.note: a sty, or pigsty, is a filthy place
U is the abbreviation for university
FF is fortissimo, the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A grimy student dive just off campus, noisy and airless.
explanation.walkthrough: The STY wraps round both U and FF together.
explanation.definitionFit: A stuffy room lacks fresh air, which is what poorly ventilated describes.

clue.text: Irrationally respect symbol of authority

indicators.note: acting irrationally means acting without order or logic, so the letters lose their order

explanation.surface: Someone holds unthinking reverence for an emblem of power.
explanation.walkthrough: SCEPTER is the American spelling of sceptre, as this is an American puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A sceptre is the ornamental staff a monarch carries as an emblem of sovereign power.

clue.text: Dangerous snafu disrupted beginning of enterprise

indicators.note: something disrupted is thrown into disorder, so its letters get rearranged
the beginning of a word is its first letter alone

explanation.surface: A perilous mix-up derails a new business at its launch.
explanation.walkthrough: Snafu is military slang for a chaotic foul-up, which fits the surface nicely.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unsafe carries a risk of harm, so it is dangerous; a plain synonym.

clue.text: Wood cube securing front of fortress in skirmish

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece holds another inside it
the front of a word is its opening letter only

explanation.surface: Siege warfare: a wooden block holding the gate of a stronghold during a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: A cube here is a number raised to the third power, and 8 is the cube of 2; EIGHT takes F inside after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A firefight is a brief exchange of gunfire between small units, a kind of skirmish.

clue.text: "Goodbye, trouble!" is heard

indicators.note: is heard means we go by the spoken sound rather than the spelling

blocks.note: ado means fuss or trouble, as in much ado about nothing

explanation.surface: Someone cheerfully waves their problems away.
explanation.walkthrough: In American speech the French farewell is commonly said much like ado.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is the French farewell used in English, meaning farewell or so long.

clue.text: Places where animals graze in unadulterated delight

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

explanation.surface: Grazing land described as a place of sheer joy.
explanation.walkthrough: A lea is a poetic word for a grassy field, so the opening phrase is wordplay, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleasure is enjoyment or gratification, the same feeling as delight.

clue.text: See 13
Will examine last word at end of fight

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: amen is said at the close of a prayer

explanation.surface: Someone will look at who gets the final say when a quarrel is over.
explanation.walkthrough: Will looks like a verb starting the sentence, but it is the noun, the legal document.
explanation.definitionFit: A testament is a legal document disposing of property after death, as in last will and testament.

clue.text: Benjamin's half — it alternates with the second half of 5 across

definitions.text: it alternates with the second half of 5 across

blocks.note: a Benjamin is US slang for a hundred-dollar bill, bearing Benjamin Franklin's portrait; half of it is a sum

blocks.clueFragment: it alternates with the second half of 5 across
blocks.note: read alternately, its letters interleave with the last three letters of the 5 across answer

explanation.walkthrough: The second half of STUFFY is FFY, and FIFTY is F, I, F, T, Y: its first, third and fifth letters are those three.
explanation.definitionFit: Half of a hundred-dollar bill is the number fifty, and its odd letters spell the end of the other entry.

clue.text: This hint to four words hidden within this puzzle's entries was not uttered by a discoverer of DNA, nor by a master decipherer of clues

definitions.text: This hint to four words hidden within this puzzle's entries was not uttered by a discoverer of DNA, nor by a master decipherer of clues

blocks.clueFragment: not uttered by a discoverer of DNA
blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation that the scientist Francis Crick never addressed to his colleague James Watson

blocks.clueFragment: nor by a master decipherer of clues
blocks.note: setter's reading: the famous line is never actually said by Sherlock Holmes in Conan Doyle's stories

explanation.walkthrough: The catchphrase is popularly credited to Sherlock Holmes but never appears in the original stories; Watson also shared the discovery of the DNA double helix with Crick.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a famous misquotation attributed to the detective, and it doubles as a hint that something simple is hidden.

clue.text: Spooner's tacky first-born gets a comfy seat

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words trade places

blocks.note: tacky is cheesy and a first-born is an heir; swap their opening sounds

explanation.surface: A tasteless eldest child is given the best armchair in the house.
explanation.definitionFit: An easy chair is a large, well-upholstered armchair, a comfortable seat.

clue.text: See 28
A monster, and therefore repulsed

indicators.note: something repulsed is driven back, so the word is read backwards

explanation.surface: A logical conclusion: it's a monster, and so people recoil from it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a man-eating giant of folklore, a kind of monster.

clue.text: Go back and forth around noon — starting a little late, feeling faint

indicators.note: starting late means the word misses its very first letter
around means one piece goes about another, enclosing it

blocks.note: to swing is to go back and forth

explanation.surface: Someone on a swing at midday, getting light-headed after a slow start.
explanation.walkthrough: SWING opens after its second letter to take in OON.
explanation.definitionFit: Swooning is fainting or nearly fainting, being overcome and light-headed.

clue.text: Part of church: section of cheap seats

indicators.note: a section is a piece cut out of a larger whole, here a run of letters

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: The cheaper pews make up one area of a church.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the rounded recess at the east end of a church, often behind the altar.

clue.text: Ocean bird harassed hat wearers

indicators.note: harassed means harried and pushed about, so the letters are disturbed

explanation.surface: A seabird swoops at people wearing hats, as gulls do at the seaside.
explanation.definitionFit: Shearwaters are long-winged seabirds that skim low over the open ocean.

clue.text: I hear the lady's outfit is covered with hair

indicators.note: I hear means the phrase is judged by how it is spoken

blocks.note: the lady's is hers, and an outfit is a suit

explanation.surface: Gossip that a woman's clothes are furry.
explanation.definitionFit: Hirsute means hairy, having a lot of hair on the body or face.

clue.text: Emile Zola, famously: "California brought up dreadful curse"

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means read from the bottom upwards
dreadful means in a terrible state, so the letters are mangled

blocks.note: CA is the postal abbreviation for California

explanation.surface: A quotation attributed to the French novelist, cursing California.
explanation.walkthrough: Zola's 1898 open letter J'accuse! charged the French army over the Dreyfus affair.
explanation.definitionFit: By publishing J'accuse, Zola publicly charged officials with injustice, making him history's best-known accuser.

clue.text: Injury is a feature of rigorous training

indicators.note: a feature of something is a part contained within it

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Getting hurt comes with tough workouts.
explanation.definitionFit: A strain is an injury caused by overstretching a muscle or tendon.

clue.text: Hipster's comeback: it is implied

indicators.note: a comeback is a coming back, so the word runs back the other way

blocks.note: cat is old jazz slang for a hip person

explanation.surface: A trendy person's retort is understood without being spelled out.
explanation.walkthrough: Comeback looks like a witty retort, but it signals reading backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit means understood without being stated, so something tacit is implied.

clue.text: Creatively recook rap to produce a kind of musical

indicators.note: doing something creatively means remaking it inventively, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Remixing hip-hop tracks to stage a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A rock opera, such as Tommy, tells a story through rock music, a type of musical.

clue.text: Former tennis champion is upset

blocks.note: Chris ..., multiple Grand Slam winner of the 1970s and 80s
to turn inside out or overturn

explanation.walkthrough: Upset looks like an adjective describing a sad player, but it is a verb meaning overturn.
explanation.definitionFit: Chris Evert won eighteen major singles titles, and evert is also a verb for turning something inside out.

clue.text: Monkeys with computer get a question half-written

indicators.note: writing only half of a word means its second half is dropped

blocks.note: a Mac is an Apple computer

explanation.surface: The old idea of monkeys at keyboards eventually typing something meaningful, here only part of a query.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaques are a genus of Old World monkeys, including the rhesus monkey.

clue.text: Times-edited articles

indicators.note: edited text is reworked and rearranged

explanation.surface: Newspaper pieces that have been through the Times's editors.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen makes Times-edited look like one adjective about a newspaper; split it into Times and edited.
explanation.definitionFit: Items are individual pieces in a newspaper, just as articles are.

clue.text: Prehistoric boast about ravaged zone at onset of epoch

indicators.note: something ravaged is wrecked, so its letters lie in disorder
about means going round, enclosing what follows
'onset of' keeps only the first letter of 'epoch'

explanation.surface: A tale of early humans bragging about a land laid waste at the dawn of an era.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bronze Age is the period before written history when bronze tools were made, so prehistoric.

clue.text: I agree to equip hothead and heavyweight

blocks.note: to rig is to fit out or equip
read as hot's head, the opening letter of hot
a ton is a great weight

explanation.surface: Agreeing to kit out a hot-tempered man and a boxer.
explanation.walkthrough: Hothead is read as hot's head, its first letter, not a short-tempered person.
explanation.definitionFit: Right on is an exclamation of enthusiastic agreement, much like saying you agree.
